sources.title: LeetCode 1488 - Avoid Flood in The City
Avoid Flood deterministic Java simulation fixture

claims.text: LeetCode 1488 defines rain days, dry days, rainy output -1, a positive lake choice on dry days, and empty output when flood avoidance is impossible.
Tracking each lake previous rain and assigning the earliest unused dry day strictly after it when the lake repeats produces a valid schedule whenever such a day exists at each deadline.
At a repeated-rain deadline, absence of any unused prior dry day strictly after the previous rain means no valid dry day exists inside the required window.
The executable simulator validates possible and impossible schedules across repeated-lake windows, unused dry days, exact windows and immediate repeats, plus defensive null/negative input handling.

findings: The repository source explicitly identifies LeetCode 1488. The official problem statement defines rain days, mandatory dry-day choices, -1 on rainy output positions, arbitrary valid dry-lake choices and empty output when avoiding flood is impossible; the candidate follows that contract without adding hidden source requirements.

The candidate state is appropriate: lastRain stores the previous fill time for each lake, while an ordered set stores past dry days that have not yet been assigned. A repeated rain creates a deadline whose required dry day must be strictly after that lake previous rain.

Using dryDays.higher(prev) selects the earliest feasible unused dry day. Since the set contains only already-observed days, the selected day is automatically before the current rain; choosing the earliest feasible day preserves later dry days for future windows with later left boundaries.
If higher(prev) does not exist at the repeated-rain deadline, no unused past dry day lies inside the required interval, so that flood is unavoidable and returning an empty array is correct.

The displayed Java is complete and matches the separately executed implementation. The deterministic simulator validates all-rain/no-repeat, a two-repeat schedule, an impossible crossing-deadline case, unused dry days, an exact one-day window, immediate repeat impossibility and defensive null/negative boundaries.

The answer explains the one-use resource/window invariant, strict higher-versus-ceiling boundary, O(n log n) TreeSet cost and alternative data-structure tradeoffs. It also keeps production experience explicitly out of scope.

No uncovered source variant, unsupported factual attribution, coding hard failure or semantic blocker remains at candidate review stage. Formal promotion remains governed by repository promotion and real-review policy.
